walkthroughs.body_html: Iceland sits astride the Mid-Atlantic Ridge with a hotspot underneath, producing frequent volcanism. Eyjafjallajökull (1,651 m) lies beneath an ice cap. The April 2010 eruption was modest (VEI 4) but interaction with ice produced fine, glassy ash carried into European airspace by prevailing winds.

Concerns about ash damaging jet engines closed much of European airspace from 15 to 21 April 2010, cancelling around 100,000 flights and affecting 10 million passengers. Estimated airline losses exceeded $1.7 billion. Perishable exports from Kenya and elsewhere also suffered.

The eruption illustrated how moderate hazards can cascade through interconnected systems. Improved ash forecasting models, revised tolerance levels for jet engines and contingency planning have since reduced disruption — but emphasise that risk assessment must account for cascading impacts as well as direct effects.
